title: Static members (type-level state and behavior)
hook: `static` belongs to the type itself, not to any single object. One copy of a static field is shared by every thread that can see the type — which is either a feature or a bug.

blocks.text: A **static member** belongs to the type, not to an instance. There is one copy of a static field shared across the entire application for that type load. A **static class** cannot be instantiated, is implicitly `sealed`, and can only contain static members. `Math` and `Console` are the textbook examples from the Base Class Library (BCL).

entries.plainDefinition: A field, method, or property that belongs to the type itself rather than to any instance.
A class that cannot be instantiated and contains only static members. Implicitly sealed.
Runs once before the first use of the type. Used to initialize static fields. Cannot be called directly.
entries.example: `static IssuerMap() { ... }` runs before the first call to any static member.

entries.plainDefinition: A compile-time value. Implicitly static. Cannot be changed at runtime.

blocks.text: Static is ideal for pure functions, frozen lookup tables, and factory methods. It is dangerous for mutable shared state in multi-threaded hosts — an SQS consumer with a static `Dictionary` that gets written at runtime is a data race unless you use concurrent types or never write after initialization.

blocks.title: Static is not dependency injection
blocks.body: A static Redis connector hides lifetime and makes unit tests lie. Prefer injecting services through constructors. Static is for stateless utilities and one-time initialization.

items.title: First reference to the type
items.body: Any call to a static member or `new` on a non-static class triggers type initialization.

items.title: Static field initializers run
items.body: In declaration order, before the static constructor body.

items.title: Static constructor runs once
items.body: The CLR guarantees it runs exactly once per type per application domain. An exception poisons the type with `TypeInitializationException`.

items.title: Static members are available
items.body: All subsequent calls use the initialized static state. No instance is ever created for a static class.

diagram.title: Static initialization flow
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  F[First static member access] --> FI[Static field initializers]
  FI --> SC[Static constructor]
  SC --> OK[Type ready]
  SC -->|exception| TIE[TypeInitializationException forever]

snippet.label: Instance vs static — what compiles
snippet.explanation: Line 4: static field shared across all instances. Line 9: static factory method. Line 11: instance methods can access static members. Line 12: static methods cannot access instance members without an instance parameter.

blocks.title: Static in C# vs JS/TS
rows: One copy per type load in metadata
JS static fields live on the constructor function
Runs once, cannot be called directly
No equivalent — use module-level `const` or IIFE
`const` is compile-time; `static readonly` is runtime once

blocks.title: Mutable static dictionaries in multi-threaded hosts
blocks.body: An SQS consumer that writes to a static `Dictionary` without locks will corrupt data. Use `ConcurrentDictionary`, initialize once as `readonly`, or inject a scoped service.

blocks.title: Static as a service locator
blocks.body: Hiding `HttpClient` or a Redis multiplexer behind static properties makes tests impossible to isolate. Register services in dependency injection instead.

interviewTakeaways: Static fields are process-wide for that type load.
Static constructors throwing poison the type with `TypeInitializationException`.
Prefer static for pure functions and frozen lookup tables, not for hidden I/O.
commonPitfalls: Mutable static dictionaries in multi-threaded hosts.
Using static as a service locator for HttpClient or multiplexers.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript static fields live on the constructor function. There is no static class that forbids `new` — only convention.
TypeScript `static` is a constructor property. C# `static` is a special member in metadata and can live on a static class with no instances allowed.
